title: ESP Course Design

pts: English for Specific Purposes is defined by a genuinely specific, identifiable learner need, not simply a themed vocabulary list.
A course teaching 'business vocabulary' generically is not automatically ESP; genuine ESP is grounded in real target-situation analysis.
This connects directly back to Unit 2's target-situation analysis, applied at full course-design scale.
points.who: Tom Hutchinson & Alan Waters, "English for Specific Purposes"

v: Two or three course outlines labelled ‘English for…’

items: Collect course outlines described as ‘English for’ a purpose: business, nursing, engineering, tourism.
For each, ask: is there evidence of a defined learner group? Of an analysis of their target situation? Of genres from the field?
Rate each outline: themed general English, partly ESP, or genuine ESP.
For the weakest outline, list three changes that would make it genuine ESP.
Share conclusions with colleagues who plan similar courses.
Evaluate the ‘communication skills’ module of a local ITI, polytechnic or nursing syllabus.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Outline A: Lesson 3: Business vocabulary (profit, loss, market, share). Grammar: present simple. → themed general English.

Outline B: Lesson 3: Handling customer complaints by phone at a bank branch. Based on recordings and interviews with branch staff. Language: apologizing, explaining procedures, escalating. → genuine ESP.
T: What does B have that A lacks?
A: A real situation and real people.
B: And someone went and found out what happens at the bank.

blocks.x: A course is ESP when it is grounded in the target situation, not when its word list has a topic label (Hutchinson and Waters 1987).

body: Purpose: to distinguish themed English from ESP. Content: two course folders: one with a large ‘Business English’ label but generic pages inside; the other with a small label but pages showing a bank counter, a phone call and a complaint form. Style: clean, contrasting. Board version: two rectangles, one with a big label and blank inside, one with a small label and three drawings inside.

items: Google Docs (free) for a shared evaluation of outlines.

pts: ESP course design typically requires more intensive needs analysis than general English — genuine workplace or academic observation, if possible.
This extends Unit 2's needs-analysis framework into its most demanding, highest-stakes application.
Involving subject-matter experts or the learners' own supervisors in this analysis, where feasible, adds crucial validity.

v: Two to four weeks, alongside teaching

items: Identify at least three sources: learners, their supervisors or employers, and a subject specialist or experienced practitioner.
Choose at least two methods: a questionnaire, semi-structured interviews, observation of the workplace or classroom, and collection of real documents (Long 2005).
Collect data on the target situation (what they must do in English), the present situation (what they can do now) and the learning situation (time, resources, preferences).
Triangulate: note where sources agree and where they conflict.
Write a one-page needs profile listing the priority tasks and genres.
If workplace observation is not possible, ask learners who are already working to keep a one-week log of every English task they meet.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Needs profile extract for a group of staff nurses in a Bengaluru private hospital (fictional):

lines: Target tasks (from supervisors and observation): shift handover; explaining discharge instructions; documenting care; phoning doctors about changes in a patient’s condition.
Present situation (from placement task): strong clinical knowledge; confident reading of charts; hesitant on the phone; handover notes often incomplete.
Conflict: nurses rated grammar as top priority; supervisors rated clear handover structure as top priority.
Decision: prioritize structured handover, with grammar focused on what handover requires.

blocks.x: Involving supervisors and subject experts adds validity that learners’ self-reports alone cannot provide.

body: Purpose: to show multi-source needs analysis. Content: a triangle with learners, employers and subject experts at its corners; at the centre, a document labelled ‘needs profile’; icons for questionnaire, interview and observation along the sides. Style: clear diagram. Board version: a triangle with three labelled corners.

items: Google Forms (free) for questionnaires.
KoboToolbox (free for humanitarian and non-profit use) for surveys that work offline on phones [VERIFY current eligibility terms].

blocks.x: Paper questionnaires and a notebook for interview and observation notes.

pts: An ESP teacher typically isn't a subject-matter expert, but needs enough genre and register awareness of the target field to teach it credibly.
This connects to Unit 55's CLIL collaboration principles — ESP practitioners often benefit from collaboration with subject specialists.
The honest acknowledgment of this role's limits, and building appropriate collaboration, produces better outcomes than overreach.

v: A subject specialist; a set of field documents

items: Identify one subject specialist willing to meet (a nursing tutor, an engineering lecturer, a hotel manager).
Before meeting, read three documents from the field and list terms and conventions you do not understand.
In the meeting, ask the specialist to explain what makes a document good or poor in their field, not only what terms mean.
Agree what you can each contribute: they bring content judgement; you bring analysis of language and genre (Unit 55).
Keep a ‘field notebook’ of what you learn, and be honest with learners about the limits of your expertise.
Invite the specialist to co-teach one lesson, or to record a short explanation of a key task.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A meeting with a nursing tutor: A (ESP teacher): What makes a handover good? B (nursing tutor): The next nurse can act on it without asking questions. Situation, background, assessment, recommendation, in that order.

lines: A: So the structure matters more than perfect grammar?
B: Yes, but vague words like ‘some’ or ‘a bit’ are dangerous. We need numbers.
A: That’s a language point I can teach: precise quantities and times.

blocks.x: An ESP teacher need not be a nurse, but needs enough genre awareness to teach nursing English credibly (Dudley-Evans and St John 1998).

body: Purpose: to show collaboration. Content: two figures at a table: one with a stethoscope and a clipboard, one with a pen and language notes; between them, a shared document labelled ‘handover lesson’. Style: warm, professional. Board version: two stick figures with one shared rectangle.

items: Google Meet or Microsoft Teams (free versions) for meetings with specialists who cannot visit.

blocks.x: A face-to-face meeting and a field notebook.

body: Dudley-Evans and St John (1998) described the ESP teacher as a ‘practitioner’ with several roles: teacher, course designer and materials provider, collaborator, researcher and evaluator. Collaboration with subject specialists can range from simple cooperation to full team teaching.

pts: Identify the specific genres a learner group actually needs — a nurse's handover report, an engineer's incident report, a diplomat's briefing note.
This applies Unit 33 and 54's genre-analysis and teaching-cycle work directly to a defined professional or academic genre set.
Real workplace or academic samples of these genres, where obtainable, are far more valuable than invented approximations.

v: Two or three real or realistic examples of one genre (anonymized)

items: Choose a priority genre from the needs profile, for example an incident report for engineering trainees.
Learners read two examples and identify the stages (moves) in each.
Label the moves and the language features typical of each (tense, passive voice, precise measurements).
Compare a strong and a weak example: which moves or features are missing in the weak one?
Learners write their own incident report from a scenario, using the move structure (Unit 54).
For spoken genres (a handover, a service call), use recordings or role-played transcripts instead of written texts.
Support: provide a move template with sentence starters.
Challenge: learners find a third example from their own workplace and analyse it independently.

blocks.x: Moves in an incident report (written for this book):

lines: Move 1, Identification: Date, time, location, equipment ID.
Move 2, Description: At 14.20, conveyor belt 3 stopped abruptly. The motor casing was found to be overheated.
Move 3, Action taken: Power was isolated. The area was cordoned off.
Move 4, Cause (if known): Preliminary inspection suggests bearing failure.
Move 5, Recommendation: Replace bearing; inspect belts 1–4 within 48 hours.
T: Which move uses the passive most?
S1: Action taken. ‘Power was isolated.’
T: Why?
S2: Because the action is important, not who did it.

blocks.x: Real workplace samples, where obtainable and anonymized, are more valuable than invented approximations.

body: Purpose: to show genre moves. Content: an incident report form with five coloured bands, each labelled with its move name and a note on typical language (for example, ‘passive’, ‘time + past simple’). Style: tidy, annotated. Board version: a rectangle divided into five labelled strips.

items: AntConc (free) to build a small corpus of field documents and find typical phrases.

blocks.x: Photocopied example reports with moves marked in pencil.

points.sub: Not narrowing too far, too soon
pts: Even a highly specific ESP course needs some general language foundation beneath its specialised content, especially at lower proficiency levels.
This connects to Unit 12's syllabus-type discussion — most ESP courses are genuinely mixed-strand rather than purely specific.
Over-narrowing too early can leave learners under-prepared for genuine communicative flexibility within their field.

v: The needs profile; a proposed course map

items: List the course’s units and mark each as general (G), specific (S) or mixed (M).
Check the learners’ current level: the lower the level, the more general foundation is usually needed.
Identify general language that the specific genres depend on (question forms for patient interviews; past tenses for reports).
Rebalance the course so that general language is taught through field contexts wherever possible.
Check that learners will still be able to handle unpredictable conversation in their field, not only fixed scripts.
In a pre-experience course (students not yet working), include more general and academic English; in an in-service course, more specific.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Course map for A2–B1 hospitality trainees (fictional):

lines: Week 1: greetings and introductions at reception (M)
Week 2: numbers, dates and times through booking calls (M)
Week 3: handling a complaint (S)
Week 4: small talk with guests about Goa (G, in a field context)
A: Should we drop small talk? It isn’t in the job description.
B: The supervisors say guests expect it. And it keeps them flexible.

blocks.x: Most ESP courses are mixed-strand (Unit 12). Narrowing too far, too early can leave learners unable to cope with the unexpected within their own field.

body: Purpose: to show the general–specific balance. Content: a dial from ‘general’ to ‘specific’ with three pointers for different groups: pre-experience A2 learners (nearer general), in-service B2 professionals (nearer specific), and a mixed group (centre). Style: clean. Board version: a semicircle with three arrows.

items: Google Sheets (free) for a colour-coded course map.

blocks.x: A course map on chart paper with G, S and M marked in different symbols.

pts: Off-the-shelf ESP materials frequently don't match a specific learner group's precise context closely enough.
This connects to Unit 41's authentic-materials-at-scale principle, applied to a professional or academic domain's real texts.
Building a materials bank specific to a recurring learner population is a worthwhile long-term institutional investment.

v: Collected field texts; a filing system

items: Collect real texts from the field: forms, manuals, emails, notices, recorded calls (with permission).
Tag each by genre, level, skill and task in a simple index.
For each text, write one or two tasks graded to the learners’ level, adapting the task rather than the text where possible (Unit 41).
Store texts and tasks in a shared folder that colleagues can use and add to.
Review the bank each year with feedback from learners and specialists.
Learners who are already working contribute texts from their own workplace, anonymized.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Text: equipment safety notice, cement plant, 1 page. Genre: notice. Level: B1. Skills: reading, mediation. Tasks: (1) identify three prohibited actions; (2) explain the notice in Kannada to a new worker (Unit 64). Source: permission from plant safety officer, 2025.

blocks.x: Off-the-shelf ESP coursebooks often do not match a specific learner group closely enough. A bank built for a recurring population is a long-term institutional investment.

body: Purpose: to show a growing institutional resource. Content: a set of labelled shelves or folders (forms, reports, calls, notices), with teachers adding documents and a small index card. Style: organized, warm. Board version: a cupboard outline with labelled shelves.

items: Google Drive (free) shared folders with a naming system.
Moodle (free, open source) for institutions that run a learning management system.

blocks.x: A labelled box file in the staff room with an index sheet.

body: Start small. Ten well-chosen real texts with good tasks are worth more than a hundred unsorted documents. Tag every text as you add it, or the bank becomes a pile.

pts: Assess against the specific target-situation performance identified in the needs analysis, not generic communicative competence measures alone.
This connects to Unit 46's task-specific rubric principle, calibrated to the field's own genuine performance standards.
Where possible, involve field-relevant stakeholders in validating what 'successful' performance actually looks like.

v: The needs profile; a draft task and rubric

items: Choose one priority task from the needs profile, such as a telephone call reporting a change in a patient’s condition.
Design an assessment task that simulates it as closely as possible: realistic prompt, time pressure, role-played interlocutor.
Draft criteria from the field’s own standards, with the specialist: completeness, accuracy of key information, structure, clarity and appropriate tone (Unit 46).
Trial the task with two learners and ask the specialist whether the higher-scoring performance would be acceptable at work.
Revise descriptors so that ‘successful’ matches what the field accepts.
Where a recognized field test exists (for example ICAO requirements or the Occupational English Test), study its public descriptions to align criteria, without claiming equivalence.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: You are the nurse on Ward 4. Mr Rao, 62, post-operative day 1, now has a temperature of 38.9°C and a pulse of 112. Phone the duty doctor.
S1: Hello doctor, I am calling about Mr Rao, Ward 4, bed 12. He had surgery yesterday. His temperature is 38.9 and pulse 112. I think he may have an infection. Can you come and see him?

blocks.x: The specialist’s verdict: ‘Clear, complete, and she made a recommendation. I would accept this at work.’ A generic speaking test would not show whether she can do this; a target-situation task does (Douglas 2000).

body: Purpose: to show target-situation assessment. Content: on the left, a real hospital ward with a nurse on the phone; on the right, a classroom role-play mirroring the scene; a line connects matching elements (phone, chart, urgency). Style: parallel scenes. Board version: two boxes with matching labels joined by lines.

items: A phone’s voice recorder (free) for recording role-played calls for assessment and feedback.

blocks.x: A role-play with a teacher or peer as interlocutor, scored live on a paper rubric.

pts: Business English, medical English, legal English, aviation English and academic English each carry genuinely distinct genre and register demands.
Each field typically has its own established professional literature and, in some cases, standardised proficiency frameworks worth consulting.
Avoid assuming expertise transfers directly between fields — genuine ESP competence is field-specific, not a single general skill.

v: Five field cards (business, medical, legal, aviation, academic)

items: Form five groups, each with a field card listing typical genres, users and any established tests or frameworks.
Groups prepare a two-minute talk on their field’s distinctive language demands, with one example.
Groups rotate in a gallery walk, adding a question or observation to each poster.
Discuss: what transfers between fields, and what does not?
Each learner or trainee chooses the field closest to their future and writes three priorities for their own English.
Replace fields with local ones: agricultural extension English, IT support English, hospitality English for Karnataka’s tourism sector.
Support: field cards include sample sentences.
Challenge: groups find one published article or report on ESP in their field.

blocks.x: Field cards (summary, written for this book):

lines: Business: emails, meetings, negotiations; directness and politeness vary across cultures.
Medical: handovers, patient explanations, notes; precision and empathy together; Occupational English Test.
Legal: contracts, affidavits; archaic and formulaic phrasing; high cost of ambiguity.
Aviation: standard radiotelephony phraseology plus plain English for non-routine events; ICAO proficiency requirements.
Academic: essays, lectures, research articles; hedging and citation (Units 61 and 62).
T: Could a good business English teacher teach aviation English tomorrow?
Ss: No.
T: Why not?
S1: Different genres, different risks. And a mistake in aviation can kill people.

blocks.x: ESP competence is field-specific; expertise in one field does not transfer automatically to another. Unit 70 draws these threads together in a full EAP/ESP course.

body: Purpose: to show common ESP fields. Content: five illustrated cards in a fan: a briefcase (business), a stethoscope (medical), a gavel (legal), an aircraft headset (aviation), a mortar board (academic), each with two keywords. Style: iconographic, balanced. Board version: five boxes with icons and labels.

items: ICAO website (free) for public information on language proficiency requirements.
Occupational English Test website (free to view) for sample task descriptions.

blocks.x: Hand-drawn field cards displayed for a gallery walk.

body: Take one course you currently teach that is labelled ‘English for…’. Interview two people who already do the job your learners are training for, and ask each to describe the three hardest English tasks in their working week. Compare their answers with your syllabus, and change one unit accordingly.

dek: Unit 65 of 100: building a course around the specific professional or academic language needs of a defined group — where general English methodology needs real adaptation.

aims.x: A nursing student in Mysuru, a polytechnic engineering trainee in Hubballi and a young hotel receptionist in Goa all need English, but not the same English. This unit shows how to design a course around the specific professional or academic needs of a defined group: English for Specific Purposes (ESP). It moves from defining ESP, through needs analysis, genre analysis and materials development, to assessment, and closes with a field guide to common ESP domains. Several points are planning tasks for teachers and course designers, because in ESP the most important work happens before the first lesson.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: explain what makes a course ESP rather than a general English course with a topic theme;
plan and carry out a needs analysis that includes target-situation observation and stakeholders;
define the role of the ESP practitioner and plan collaboration with subject specialists;
identify and analyse the key genres a learner group needs;
balance general and specific language according to learners’ level and goals;
develop and organize a bank of materials based on real workplace or academic texts;
design assessment tasks that reflect target-situation performance;
describe the distinctive demands of several common ESP fields.

why: Why this matters. A generic communicative course underserves learners with narrow, specific, high-stakes language needs — a nurse, an engineer, a diplomat each need genuinely different English.

background.x: Tom Hutchinson and Alan Waters (1987) summarized the ESP principle in one sentence: tell me what you need English for and I will tell you the English that you need. ESP is an approach, not a product: it begins with learners’ reasons for learning. Tony Dudley-Evans and Maggie Jo St John (1998) added that ESP is defined by the specific needs of learners and makes use of the methodology and activities of the discipline it serves. A course called ‘Business English’ that teaches a generic list of business words is not necessarily ESP; a course built on an analysis of what a particular group of bank clerks must read, write, say and understand is.

The foundation of ESP is needs analysis. John Munby (1978) proposed a detailed communicative needs processor for describing target situations; later writers made the idea more practical. Michael Long (2005) argued for task-based needs analysis using multiple sources (learners, employers, domain experts, documents) and multiple methods (interviews, questionnaires, observation). Dudley-Evans and St John distinguished target-situation analysis (what learners must do in English) from present-situation analysis (what they can do now) and learning-situation analysis (how they prefer and are able to learn). This builds directly on the needs analysis introduced in Unit 2.

The second foundation is genre analysis (Swales 1990; Unit 33 and Unit 54). Each profession has typical texts and spoken events: a nurse’s shift handover, an engineer’s incident report, a lawyer’s affidavit, a pilot’s radio exchange. Helen Basturkmen (2010) showed how ESP course designers can analyse these genres and turn them into teachable units. Assessment follows the same logic. Dan Douglas (2000) argued that specific-purpose tests should reflect the context and tasks of the target situation, and several fields now have their own tests, such as the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) language proficiency requirements for pilots and air traffic controllers and the Occupational English Test for health professionals.

India has an enormous and growing ESP need. Skill-development programmes, Industrial Training Institutes, polytechnics, nursing colleges, engineering colleges and hospitality institutes all include English, often as ‘communication skills’ or ‘employability skills’. NEP 2020 emphasizes vocational education and its integration with general education (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020). Many learners in these programmes studied in Kannada, Marathi or Bengali medium, and bring deep knowledge of their field alongside limited English. An ESP course that respects their subject knowledge and uses their home languages strategically (Unit 64) can move them quickly from what they know to how to say it in English.

items: Needs profile. A one-page profile for a defined learner group, based on at least three sources and two methods.
Genre analysis. A move analysis of one priority genre, with language features and a teaching sequence.
Course map. A general–specific course map with a rationale for the balance chosen.
Target-situation task. An assessment task and rubric validated with a subject specialist.
Which of your courses called ‘English for…’ would pass the test of being genuine ESP?
Whose voices were missing from the last needs analysis you did?
How comfortable are you teaching a field you do not know? Who could you collaborate with?
How do you balance general flexibility against specific, high-stakes tasks?
What real texts from your learners’ fields could you begin collecting this term?
How do learners’ home languages and subject knowledge support their ESP learning?

perm: Real workplace documents must be anonymized, and permission obtained from the organization before use in class or publication.

All needs profiles, reports, prompts, course maps and dialogues are original and written for this book; patient and workplace details are fictional. Real workplace documents require anonymization and the organization’s permission. Descriptions of ICAO requirements and the Occupational English Test are summaries; consult the official sources and do not reproduce test materials. Screenshots of Google Forms, KoboToolbox, AntConc, Google Drive, Moodle or Google Meet require permission or replacement with original illustrations.

terms.def: Teaching English for a particular professional or academic need, such as nursing, engineering or hospitality, with content and tasks drawn from analysis of the learners’ target situations (Hutchinson and Waters 1987).
Analysing examples of a genre to identify its purpose, typical moves or stages and characteristic language, so that learners can be taught to produce it (Swales 1990).

In course design, especially ESP, the analysis of the conditions in which a course will run, such as time available, class size, resources, and teachers’ and learners’ expectations, alongside analysis of target needs.
An organized, growing collection of texts, tasks and resources, often gathered from the target field in ESP, that teachers can draw on and share when planning courses.
In genre analysis, a stage of a text that performs a recognizable communicative function, such as ‘establishing a territory’ at the start of a research article introduction (Swales 1990).
In ESP course design, the analysis of learners’ current language abilities, resources and learning situation at the start of a course.

Assessment that reflects the contexts and tasks of learners’ target situation, such as a nurse’s shift handover or an engineer’s report (Douglas 2000). It is used in English for Specific Purposes courses.
An expert in the learners’ professional or academic field, such as a nurse, engineer or lawyer, with whom an ESP teacher collaborates on needs analysis, materials and assessment.

The part of needs analysis that identifies what learners will need to do in English in their target situation, including tasks, texts and skills (Hutchinson and Waters 1987). It is paired with present-situation analysis.

Using several sources, methods or perspectives to check findings, for example combining learner interviews, employer views and document analysis in needs analysis, or observation and learner work in action research.
